h: Tips, timings and a bit of village tradition
p: Visits are guided, and the guides are a big part of the fun. Expect plenty of stories about the ropemakers, the cave's colourful history and how it got its nickname. Children love the cheeky name, and the guides know exactly how to play it for laughs while still slipping in plenty of real history.

Wrap up warm, as the cave is cool all year, and wear sensible shoes, because parts of the route are uneven and can be damp. If you're short on time, combining Peak Cavern with Speedwell Cavern on the same day is a popular choice, giving you one walking cave and one boat trip underground for a nice contrast.

The cave entrance sits in a dramatic gorge right below the ruins of Peveril Castle, built by William Peverel in the years after the Norman Conquest. The castle is now looked after by English Heritage, and the climb up rewards you with brilliant views over the village and Hope Valley.

Castleton has some lovely traditions too. Garland Day is held around the end of May, when a rider in a huge garland of flowers leads a procession through the streets. If your visit happens to coincide, it's a really memorable bit of local character.

After the cave, take a wander round the village shops, many of which sell Blue John jewellery and ornaments, then settle into one of the pubs or tea rooms for something warming. It's an easy place to spend a whole day, and an even easier place to come back to.
